q: When is the Island ferry busiest?

queries.purpose: Average riders per day by month (complete years 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(d, '%b') AS label, round(avg(day_total)) AS value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, sum(tickets_redeemed) AS day_total FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY month(d), strftime(d, '%b') ORDER BY month(d)

queries.purpose: Average riders per day by day of week (summer, Jun-Aug, 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(d, '%a') AS label, round(avg(day_total)) AS value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, sum(tickets_redeemed) AS day_total FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 AND month(ts) IN (6,7,8) GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY isodow(d), strftime(d, '%a') ORDER BY isodow(d)

queries.purpose: Average riders per hour of day (summer, Jun-Aug, 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT lpad(CAST(h AS VARCHAR), 2, '0') || ':00' AS label, round(sum(tickets_redeemed) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT d)) AS value FROM (SELECT hour(ts) AS h, date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, tickets_redeemed FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 AND month(ts) IN (6,7,8)) GROUP BY h ORDER BY h

story.lead: Summer Saturdays around noon are busiest.
story.sub: Island ferry tickets redeemed, complete years 2016-2025, in 15-minute counts added up by day and hour.

points.h: August is the busiest month
points.p: Riders per day climb from spring to a peak in August, then fall quickly.
points.more: August averages 9,768 riders a day and July 8,699. January is the quietest at 492 a day.

points.h: Weekends are far busier than weekdays
points.p: In summer, Saturday and Sunday carry about double the weekday crowds.
points.more: Saturday averages 12,513 riders and Sunday 11,518. Tuesday is the lowest at 5,521, and Friday is the busiest weekday at 7,257.

points.h: Midday is the peak time
points.p: On summer days, ridership builds through the morning and peaks around noon.
points.more: The 12:00 hour averages 995 riders, with 11:00 close at 986. By 18:00 it falls to 341, and before 08:00 it is under 60 an hour.

q: Which subway stations have the most delays?

queries.purpose: Stations with the most delays (incidents with delay minutes above 0)
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, count(*) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Stations with the most total delay minutes
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, sum(min_delay) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Stations with the longest average delay (stations with at least 30 delays)
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, round(avg(min_delay), 1) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station HAVING count(*) >= 30 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

story.lead: Kipling station has the most delays.
story.sub: TTC subway delay incidents with delay minutes above 0, January 2025 to August 2026.

stat.caption: delays at Kipling station, the most of any station

points.h: Kipling, Kennedy and Wilson lead on delay count
points.p: Kipling station had the most delays, followed closely by Kennedy and Wilson.
points.more: Kipling had 578 delays, Kennedy (Line 2) 537, Wilson 513 and Bloor 504. Finch had 464 and Eglinton 446.

points.h: Eglinton loses the most minutes overall
points.p: Eglinton station tops the list for total minutes of delay.
points.more: Eglinton added up to 4,001 minutes, ahead of Kipling at 3,461 and Kennedy at 3,136. Victoria Park and Sheppard West each passed 3,000 minutes despite fewer delays.

points.h: Woodbine has the longest typical delay
points.p: Among stations with at least 30 delays, Woodbine delays last longest on average.
points.more: Woodbine averaged 12.3 minutes per delay, then Sheppard West at 12 and Islington at 11.9. Eglinton averaged 9 minutes.

q: What are the most popular dog names?

queries.purpose: Top 15 dog names in 2025 by licensed dogs
queries.sql: SELECT upper(left(name, 1)) || lower(substr(name, 2)) AS label, licensed_count AS value FROM pet_names WHERE animal = 'DOG' AND year = 2025 ORDER BY licensed_count DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 dog names, average licensed dogs per year 2020-2025
queries.sql: SELECT upper(left(name, 1)) || lower(substr(name, 2)) AS label, round(avg(licensed_count)) AS value FROM pet_names WHERE animal = 'DOG' AND year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025 GROUP BY name ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: How the most popular name has changed year by year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, licensed_count AS value FROM pet_names WHERE animal = 'DOG' AND year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025 AND name = (SELECT name FROM pet_names WHERE animal = 'DOG' AND year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025 GROUP BY name ORDER BY sum(licensed_count) DESC LIMIT 1) ORDER BY year

story.lead: Luna and Charlie are Toronto's top dog names.
story.sub: Licensed dogs in Toronto, 2020 to 2025 (top 200 names per year only).

stat.caption: licensed dogs named Luna in 2025, the most of any name

points.h: Luna led the 2025 dog names
points.p: Luna was the most common name among licensed dogs in 2025, ahead of Charlie.
points.more: Luna had 549 dogs and Charlie 491. Bella was third with 386, then Coco with 342 and Milo with 315.

points.h: Charlie leads over the six years
points.p: Averaged over 2020 to 2025, Charlie comes first and Luna second.
points.more: Charlie averaged 529 dogs a year and Luna 493. Bella was third at 405. Max, Coco and Daisy followed.

points.h: Charlie has slipped since 2021
points.p: The top name over the six years, Charlie, peaked in 2021 and has been lower since.
points.more: Charlie went from 595 dogs in 2021 to 491 in 2025. It was 553 in 2020 and 488 in 2024.

queries.purpose: Most common recorded causes of fires, 2011-2024
queries.sql: SELECT regexp_replace(possible_cause, '^[0-9]+ - ', '') AS label, count(*) AS value FROM fire_incidents WHERE incident_type LIKE '01%' AND possible_cause IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 12

rows.label: Improper handling of ignition source or ignited material

queries.purpose: Known causes only (excluding undetermined/unknown)
queries.sql: SELECT regexp_replace(possible_cause, '^[0-9]+ - ', '') AS label, count(*) AS value FROM fire_incidents WHERE incident_type LIKE '01%' AND possible_cause IS NOT NULL AND possible_cause NOT LIKE '99%' AND possible_cause NOT LIKE '88%' AND possible_cause NOT ILIKE '%undetermined%' AND possible_cause NOT ILIKE '%under investigation%' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 12

rows.label: Improper handling of ignition source or ignited material
Routine maintenance deficiency, eg creosote, lint, grease buildup

queries.purpose: Causes of fires in homes with deadly or serious impact: civilian casualties by cause
queries.sql: SELECT regexp_replace(possible_cause, '^[0-9]+ - ', '') AS label, sum(civilian_casualties) AS value FROM fire_incidents WHERE incident_type LIKE '01%' AND possible_cause IS NOT NULL AND possible_cause NOT LIKE '99%' GROUP BY 1 HAVING sum(civilian_casualties) > 0 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 10

rows.label: Improper handling of ignition source or ignited material
Used or Placed too close to combustibles
Other misuse of ignition source/material ignited

story.lead: Electrical failure is the top known fire cause.
story.sub: Fires Toronto Fire Services attended, 2011 to 2024, by the cause recorded for each fire.

stat.caption: fires blamed on electrical failure, the top known cause, 2011-2024

points.h: Most fires have an undetermined cause
points.p: The most common entry is Undetermined, with 4,012 fires, ahead of electrical failure at 3,134.
points.more: Improperly discarded items follow with 2,255 fires, then other unintended cause (1,990) and unattended (1,928). Several of the listed causes are similar catch-all labels.

points.h: Electrical failure leads among known causes
points.p: With unknown causes removed, electrical failure is still first at 3,134 fires.
points.more: Improperly discarded (2,255) and other unintended cause (1,990) come next. Unattended is fourth with 1,928 fires. Intentional fires are 617.

points.h: Unattended fires cause the most civilian casualties
points.p: Unattended fires are linked to 350 civilian casualties, more than any other cause.
points.more: That is about double the next cause, improper handling of ignition source or ignited material (170). Electrical failure is third with 164, and improperly discarded is fifth with 118.

story.lead: The 504 King is the most-delayed streetcar route.
story.sub: TTC streetcar delay records, 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026, counting only incidents with at least one minute of delay.

stat.caption: total delay minutes on the 504 King, the most of any route

points.h: 504 King and 501 Queen are nearly tied
points.p: The 504 King had 3,269 delays, just ahead of the 501 Queen with 3,255.
points.more: The 505 Dundas (2,491) and 506 Carlton (2,349) come next. The 503 Kingston Road has 1,552, and every other route has fewer than 1,400.

points.h: 504 King loses the most time overall
points.p: Added up, delays on the 504 King cost 77,703 minutes, more than any other route.
points.more: The 501 Queen follows with 74,034 minutes, then the 505 Dundas with 59,316 and the 506 Carlton with 56,379. The top four routes are well ahead of the rest.

points.h: Night routes have the longest delays
points.p: Night routes average the most minutes per delay, led by the 301 Queen Night at 35.
points.more: Among day routes, the 506 Carlton averages 24 minutes, with the 505 Dundas and 504 King both at 23.8. The 510 Spadina has the shortest at 14.9 minutes.

queries.purpose: Average people in shelters per night, by year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(date) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(avg(n)) AS value FROM (SELECT date, sum(service_users) AS n FROM shelter_occupancy GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY year(date) ORDER BY year(date)

queries.purpose: Average people per night by month, last 24 months of full data
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(m, '%b %Y') AS label, value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS m, round(avg(n)) AS value FROM (SELECT date, sum(service_users) AS n FROM shelter_occupancy WHERE date < DATE '2026-10-01' GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 24) ORDER BY m

queries.purpose: Average people per night by sector, 2025
queries.sql: SELECT sector AS label, round(avg(n)) AS value FROM (SELECT date, sector, sum(service_users) AS n FROM shelter_occupancy WHERE year(date) = 2025 GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY sector ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: About 7,300 people a night now, down from peak.
story.sub: Nightly shelter totals, Jan 2021 to Oct 2026 (2026 is a partial year); monthly view covers Oct 2024 to Sep 2026.

stat.caption: average people in shelters per night in September 2026

points.h: Nightly numbers peaked in 2024, then fell
points.p: The yearly average rose from 6,382 in 2021 to 9,766 in 2024, then dropped.
points.more: 2025 averaged 9,215 people a night. So far in 2026 the average is 8,209, which is about 1,550 below the 2024 peak.

points.h: Numbers have fallen steadily over two years
points.p: Monthly averages were above 10,000 in early 2025 and are now near 7,300.
points.more: January 2025 was the high at 10,228 a night. September 2026 was the low at 7,324. Each winter was higher than the months before and after it, but the 2026 winter peak (9,217) was below the 2025 one.

points.h: Mixed adult shelters held the most people
points.p: In 2025, mixed adult programs averaged 2,831 people a night, ahead of every other group.
points.more: Families came next at 2,484, then men at 2,099 and women at 1,082. Youth had the fewest at 719 a night.

queries.purpose: Share of beach-days with E. coli over 100 (unsafe), last 5 seasons
queries.sql: SELECT beach AS label, round(100.0 * avg(CASE WHEN d_ecoli > 100 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 1) AS value FROM (SELECT beach, date, avg(ecoli) AS d_ecoli FROM beach_water WHERE ecoli IS NOT NULL AND date >= DATE '2021-01-01' GROUP BY beach, date) GROUP BY beach HAVING count(*) >= 30 ORDER BY value ASC LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Typical (median) E. coli level per beach, last 5 seasons
queries.sql: SELECT beach AS label, round(median(d_ecoli), 1) AS value FROM (SELECT beach, date, avg(ecoli) AS d_ecoli FROM beach_water WHERE ecoli IS NOT NULL AND date >= DATE '2021-01-01' GROUP BY beach, date) GROUP BY beach HAVING count(*) >= 30 ORDER BY value ASC LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Days sampled per beach, to show how much data backs each result
queries.sql: SELECT beach AS label, count(*) AS value FROM (SELECT beach, date FROM beach_water WHERE ecoli IS NOT NULL AND date >= DATE '2021-01-01' GROUP BY beach, date) GROUP BY beach ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 30

story.lead: Gibraltar Point Beach is the safest for swimming.
story.sub: Based on E. coli samples at 10 Toronto beaches, swimming seasons from 2021 to 2026.

stat.caption: of sampled days Gibraltar Point Beach was over the unsafe limit of 100

points.h: Gibraltar Point has the fewest unsafe days
points.p: Gibraltar Point Beach was unsafe on 4.3% of sampled days, the lowest of any beach.
points.more: Hanlan's Point (6.6%) and Cherry Beach (7.7%) follow. Sunnyside Beach was worst at 36.8%, with Marie Curtis Park East (35.7%) and Centre Island (35.3%) close behind.

points.h: Four beaches share the lowest typical level
points.p: Gibraltar Point, Ward's Island, Hanlan's Point and Cherry Beach all have a median of 14 E. coli per 100 mL.
points.more: Sunnyside Beach has the highest median at 74, about five times higher. Bluffer's Beach Park (22) and Woodbine Beaches (26) are the next best.

points.h: Every beach has about 600 or more sampled days
points.p: Each beach was sampled on at least 601 days, so the comparison rests on a lot of readings.
points.more: Woodbine Beaches has the most, at 651 days. Gibraltar Point has the fewest, at 601, which is still plenty.

queries.purpose: Pothole requests per year (2026 partial, Jan-Aug)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(date) AS VARCHAR) AS label, sum(requests) AS value FROM service_requests_311 WHERE request_type ILIKE '%pot%hole%' OR request_type ILIKE '%pothole%' GROUP BY year(date) ORDER BY year(date)

queries.purpose: Pothole requests by month, average across all years (seasonality)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(date, '%b') AS label, round(sum(requests) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT year(date))) AS value FROM service_requests_311 WHERE request_type ILIKE '%pot%hole%' OR request_type ILIKE '%pothole%' GROUP BY month(date), strftime(date, '%b') ORDER BY month(date)

queries.purpose: Pothole requests by month, last 24 months
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(m, '%b %Y') AS label, value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS m, sum(requests) AS value FROM service_requests_311 WHERE (request_type ILIKE '%pot%hole%' OR request_type ILIKE '%pothole%') AND date >= DATE '2024-09-01' AND date < DATE '2026-09-01' GROUP BY 1) ORDER BY m

story.lead: Pothole complaints jumped to a record in 2026.
story.sub: 311 pothole requests, Jan 2019 to Aug 2026; 2026 covers only Jan to Aug.

stat.caption: pothole requests in just the first eight months of 2026

points.h: 2026 already tops every full year
points.p: Yearly pothole requests have swung up and down, and 2026 is the highest so far.
points.more: The 2026 total of 23,976 is already above 2019, the highest full year, at 18,495. The lowest year was 2021, at 4,432.

points.h: Complaints peak in late winter
points.p: On average, requests climb in February and peak in March, then fade through the year.
points.more: March averages 2,706 requests a year, against 359 in November, the quietest month. February and April are the next busiest at 1,962 and 1,851.

points.h: Early 2026 far outpaced early 2025
points.p: The last two springs both peaked in March, but 2026 was much bigger.
points.more: March 2026 had 6,227 requests, against 3,250 in March 2025. February 2026 reached 5,067, against 1,244 a year earlier. By August 2026, the monthly count had dropped to 629.

story.lead: Lawrence West is the most-delayed bus route.
story.sub: TTC bus delay incidents with at least one minute of delay, 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026.

stat.caption: delays on the 52 Lawrence West, the most of any bus route

points.h: 52 Lawrence West has the most delays
points.p: The 52 Lawrence West had more delay incidents than any other bus route.
points.more: It had 2,179 delays, ahead of the 102 Markham Road with 1,904 and the 32 Eglinton West with 1,878. The 15th route on the list, the 165 Weston Road North, still had 1,357.

points.h: Lawrence West also loses the most minutes
points.p: By total minutes lost, the 52 Lawrence West is first again, with the 97 Yonge close behind.
points.more: The 52 Lawrence West lost 48,648 minutes and the 97 Yonge lost 47,951. The 97 Yonge is not in the top 15 for number of delays, so its delays must be long ones. The 29 Dufferin is third with 42,364 minutes.

points.h: A few routes have very long delays
points.p: Some routes have far longer average delays than the busiest ones, among routes with at least 100 delays.
points.more: The 162 Lawrence-Donway averages 106.5 minutes per delay and the 77 Swansea 86.3. The 55 Warren Park comes third at 70.6 minutes. The 15th route on this list still averages 50.7 minutes.

story.lead: About 40 cyclists a year are seriously hurt.
story.sub: Cyclists killed or seriously injured in Toronto collisions, 2006 to 2025, from the City's KSI collision data.

stat.caption: cyclists killed or seriously injured in 2025

points.h: Yearly numbers have mostly stayed between 33 and 52
points.p: Cyclists killed or seriously injured peaked in 2012 and were lowest in 2021.
points.more: The peak was 68 people in 2012, and the low was 21 in 2021. Since then the count rose to 45 in 2023, then fell to 43 in 2024 and 33 in 2025.

points.h: Deaths are few, but 2024 stood out
points.p: Between 1 and 7 cyclists were killed each year.
points.more: 2024 had 7 deaths, the most in any year shown. 2025 had 2, and 2023 and 2021 each had 1.

points.h: Summer is the most dangerous time
points.p: Most cyclist serious injuries happen from May to September.
points.more: June averaged 5.5 people a year and July 5.4. January and February averaged just 0.8 each.

story.lead: Very few: only 82 inspections ended in a closure.
story.sub: Based on DineSafe inspections from November 2023 to early October 2026; closures appear from January 2024 to September 2026.

stat.caption: inspections ended in a closure, about 1 in 1,000

points.h: Closures stay in single digits each month

story.lead: July is the busiest month for marriage licences.
story.sub: Marriage licences issued in Toronto, monthly, 2011 to 2025 (full years only). Licences are a sign of weddings, not a count of them.

stat.caption: average licences issued in July, 2011 to 2025

points.h: July and August lead; winter is quietest
points.p: Licences climb from winter to a peak in July, then drop after August.
points.more: July averages 1,995 licences and August 1,938. December is the lowest at 730, with January at 767 and November at 801.

points.h: Recent years show the same summer peak
points.p: From 2022 to 2025, July is still on top, with August close behind.
points.more: July averages 2,166 licences and August 2,101, both higher than the long-run averages. December is lowest at 750.

points.h: Toronto City Hall issues over half of all licences
points.p: City Hall issues far more licences each year than the other three civic centres.
points.more: Toronto City Hall averages 8,374 licences a year, North York 3,379, Scarborough 2,034 and Etobicoke 1,308. This is a yearly average across all months.

queries.sql: SELECT CAST(ward AS VARCHAR) AS label, count(*) AS value FROM street_trees WHERE common_name = 'Maple, Norway' AND ward IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ward ORDER BY ward LIMIT 30

story.lead: Norway maple is the most common street tree.
story.sub: Based on the current inventory of 688,335 City-owned street trees in Toronto, as downloaded in October 2026.

stat.caption: Norway maple street trees, more than any other type

points.h: Norway maple far ahead of other trees
points.p: Norway maple has 69,468 street trees, the most of any type.
points.more: Honey locust is next with 27,758, then Colorado blue spruce with 24,086. Norway maple has about 2.5 times as many as honey locust. Honey locust also shows up as two more varieties, Skyline (16,227) and Shademaster (11,773).

points.h: Maples are the biggest group by genus
points.p: The maple genus, Acer, has 185,621 street trees, the most of any genus.
points.more: Next are honey locust (Gleditsia) with 59,904 and oak (Quercus) with 51,575. Linden (Tilia) has 46,275 and spruce (Picea) has 41,128.

points.h: Norway maples are found in every ward
points.p: Every ward has Norway maples, but the numbers vary a lot between wards.
points.more: Ward 2 has the most with 7,606, followed by ward 15 with 5,104 and ward 3 with 4,738. Wards 13 and 10 have the fewest, with 693 and 700.

queries.purpose: Top 15 branches by visits in 2024
queries.sql: SELECT branch AS label, visits AS value FROM library_visits WHERE year = 2024 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 branches by average yearly visits, 2012-2024
queries.sql: SELECT branch AS label, round(avg(visits)) AS value FROM (SELECT branch, year, sum(visits) AS visits FROM library_visits GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY branch ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Total visits across all branches per year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, sum(visits) AS value FROM library_visits GROUP BY year ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: North York Central is the busiest branch.
story.sub: Toronto Public Library visits per branch, 2012 to 2024, with a closer look at 2024.

points.h: Two big libraries lead 2024 by a wide margin
points.p: North York Central and the Toronto Reference Library each had over 1.1 million visits in 2024.
points.more: The next branch, Bloor/Gladstone, had 272,078 visits. That is roughly a fifth of North York Central's 1,276,231.

points.h: Over 2012 to 2024, the Reference Library leads
points.p: Averaged across all years, the Toronto Reference Library comes first, with North York Central close behind.
points.more: The Reference Library averaged 1,126,591 visits a year and North York Central 1,094,294. Fairview is third at 353,584, and Woodside Square, Bridlewood and Bloor/Gladstone follow.

points.h: Total visits are still below the 2012 level
points.p: Visits across all branches fell sharply in 2020 and 2021 and have been rising since.
points.more: Visits were 18,872,613 in 2012 and 17,248,761 in 2019. They dropped to 4,029,488 in 2021, then climbed to 13,431,636 in 2024.

q: How fast does Toronto Fire arrive?

queries.purpose: Typical (median) response time by year, all calls
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(alarm_time) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(median(response_minutes), 1) AS value FROM fire_calls WHERE response_minutes IS NOT NULL AND response_minutes >= 0 GROUP BY year(alarm_time) ORDER BY year(alarm_time) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Typical (median) response time by type of call
queries.sql: SELECT call_type AS label, round(median(response_minutes), 1) AS value FROM fire_calls WHERE response_minutes IS NOT NULL AND response_minutes >= 0 GROUP BY call_type ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Typical (median) response time by hour of day
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(hour(alarm_time) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(median(response_minutes), 1) AS value FROM fire_calls WHERE response_minutes IS NOT NULL AND response_minutes >= 0 GROUP BY hour(alarm_time) ORDER BY hour(alarm_time) LIMIT 30

story.lead: Toronto Fire typically arrives in about five minutes.
story.sub: Based on every Toronto Fire call with a recorded response time, 2018 to 2024.

stat.caption: typical (median) response time in 2024, alarm to first truck arriving

points.h: Response time has barely changed since 2018
points.p: The typical response stayed between 4.9 and 5.3 minutes every year.
points.more: It was 4.9 minutes in 2018 and 2019, peaked at 5.3 in 2022, and was 5.1 in both 2023 and 2024.

points.h: Medical and fire calls get the quickest response
points.p: Medical and emergency fire calls both have a typical response of 5 minutes.
points.more: Carbon monoxide and hazardous materials calls take 6 minutes. Non-emergency calls take longest at 7.4 minutes.

points.h: Overnight responses are slower than daytime ones
points.p: Typical response is 4.9 minutes through most of the day but longer overnight.
points.more: It reaches 5.8 minutes between 3 and 5 am. It drops to 5 minutes by 7 am and stays near 4.9 through the evening.

queries.purpose: Registered short-term rental operators by ward
queries.sql: SELECT coalesce(ward_name, 'Unknown') || ' (' || CAST(ward AS VARCHAR) || ')' AS label, count(*) AS value FROM short_term_rentals WHERE ward IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ward, ward_name ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 25

queries.purpose: Condominium registrations by ward
queries.sql: SELECT coalesce(ward_name, 'Unknown') || ' (' || CAST(ward AS VARCHAR) || ')' AS label, count(*) AS value FROM short_term_rentals WHERE ward IS NOT NULL AND property_type = 'Condominium' GROUP BY ward, ward_name ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 25

queries.purpose: Houses (single/semi-detached) registrations by ward
queries.sql: SELECT coalesce(ward_name, 'Unknown') || ' (' || CAST(ward AS VARCHAR) || ')' AS label, count(*) AS value FROM short_term_rentals WHERE ward IS NOT NULL AND property_type = 'Single/Semi-detached House' GROUP BY ward, ward_name ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 25

story.lead: Spadina-Fort York has the most short-term rentals.
story.sub: Current snapshot of registered short-term rental operators across Toronto's 25 wards, downloaded October 2026.

stat.caption: registered operators in Spadina-Fort York, the most of any ward

points.h: Downtown wards dominate registrations
points.p: Spadina-Fort York has 2,669 registrations, far ahead of every other ward.
points.more: Toronto Centre (984) and University-Rosedale (827) come next. These three wards hold about 51% of all 8,742 registrations. Scarborough North has the fewest at 64.

points.h: Condos explain the downtown lead
points.p: Spadina-Fort York has 2,171 condominium registrations, well ahead of any other ward.
points.more: That is about 81% of the ward's registrations. Toronto Centre has 668 condos and University-Rosedale 343. Most wards have fewer than 30.

points.h: Houses are spread across more wards
points.p: Davenport leads house registrations with 341, followed by Toronto-Danforth with 288.
points.more: Parkdale-High Park (263) and Beaches-East York (262) follow. Spadina-Fort York has only 89 houses, and Toronto Centre has 73.

queries.purpose: New dwelling units created by permits issued each year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(issued_date) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(sum(units_created)) AS value FROM building_permits WHERE issued_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND issued_date < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY year(issued_date) ORDER BY year(issued_date)

queries.purpose: Net new homes each year (created minus lost)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(issued_date) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(sum(coalesce(units_created,0) - coalesce(units_lost,0))) AS value FROM building_permits WHERE issued_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND issued_date < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY year(issued_date) ORDER BY year(issued_date)

queries.purpose: Homes created by type of structure, 2017-2025
queries.sql: SELECT structure_type AS label, round(sum(units_created)) AS value FROM building_permits WHERE issued_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND issued_date < DATE '2026-01-01' AND structure_type IS NOT NULL GROUP BY structure_type HAVING sum(units_created) > 0 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 12

story.lead: Permits created 87,639 homes, peaking in 2021.
story.sub: Building permits issued 2017 to 2025 that are now closed or finished, counting dwelling units created.

points.h: New homes peaked in 2021, then fell
points.p: Homes created by permits rose to 15,109 in 2021, then dropped each year to 2,063 in 2025.
points.more: 2020 had 14,184 homes and 2018 had 13,126. After 2023 (9,311), the count fell to 4,180 in 2024 and 2,063 in 2025.

points.h: Net new homes follow the same pattern
points.p: After subtracting homes lost, the yearly totals are lower but rise and fall the same way.
points.more: Net new homes were highest in 2021 at 13,565 and lowest in 2025 at 1,363. In 2025, 700 homes were lost against 2,063 created.

points.h: Mixed-use and apartment buildings dominate
points.p: Most new homes came from mixed-use buildings and apartment buildings, not houses.
points.more: Mixed use with shops or offices added 39,798 homes and apartment buildings 28,518, together 68,316. Detached houses added 6,073 and laneway or rear yard suites added 921.

story.lead: Bin repairs, missed pickups and wildlife lead 311 calls.
story.sub: 311 service requests in Toronto, January 2019 to August 2026, with a closer look at 2025.

stat.caption: requests to Solid Waste Management Services, the busiest City division

points.h: Damaged bin lids top the all-time list
points.p: Repairing or replacing a bin lid is the single most common request type, with 101,371 requests.
points.more: Property Standards (81,495) and injured wildlife (73,186) come next. Pothole repair has 62,390 requests. Because names changed in 2025, the renamed bin lid type adds another 37,270 on its own line.

points.h: Garbage and waste make up the biggest share
points.p: Solid Waste Management Services handles more requests than any other division, at 1,133,635.
points.more: Transportation Services follows with 800,318 and Municipal Licensing & Standards with 749,891. Toronto Water has 271,647. Solid Waste alone is about 36% of all requests.

points.h: In 2025, bin lids and property standards led
points.p: Damaged bin lids led 2025 with 24,448 requests, ahead of property standards at 17,079.
points.more: Wildlife was next: dead wildlife pickup (15,513) and injured wildlife (15,192). Potholes had 11,304 requests and sidewalk snow clearing 10,241.

queries.purpose: 15 lowest-scoring buildings (latest evaluation)
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT address AS label, round(score, 1) AS value FROM apartment_evaluations WHERE score IS NOT NULL AND address IS NOT NULL QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY address ORDER BY evaluation_date DESC) = 1 ORDER BY score ASC LIMIT 15) ORDER BY value DESC

queries.purpose: Average latest score by owner type
queries.sql: SELECT CASE property_type WHEN 'TCHC' THEN 'Toronto Community Housing' WHEN 'SOCIAL HOUSING' THEN 'Social housing' WHEN 'PRIVATE' THEN 'Private' ELSE property_type END AS label, round(avg(score), 1) AS value FROM (SELECT * FROM apartment_evaluations WHERE score IS NOT NULL AND address IS NOT NULL QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY address ORDER BY evaluation_date DESC) = 1) GROUP BY property_type ORDER BY value DESC

queries.purpose: Wards with the lowest average building score
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT ward_name AS label, round(avg(score), 1) AS value FROM (SELECT * FROM apartment_evaluations WHERE score IS NOT NULL AND address IS NOT NULL AND ward_name IS NOT NULL QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY address ORDER BY evaluation_date DESC) = 1) GROUP BY ward_name ORDER BY avg(score) ASC LIMIT 10) ORDER BY value DESC

story.lead: 2 Prospect St scores lowest, at 18 out of 100.
story.sub: Latest RentSafeTO evaluation of each apartment building, June 2023 to October 2026.

points.h: Two buildings fall far below the rest
points.p: 2 Prospect St (18) and 711 Bloor St W (23) are the two lowest scores.
points.more: The next lowest are 500 Dawes Rd and 15 Gore Vale Ave, both at 45. The 15th lowest building scores 62, so the bottom 15 span from 18 to 62.

points.h: Owner type makes almost no difference
points.p: Average scores are very close across all three owner types.
points.more: Social housing averages 91, private buildings 90.5 and Toronto Community Housing 90.4. That is a gap of only 0.6 points.

points.h: Even the lowest wards average 86 or more
points.p: The ten lowest wards all average between 86 and 90.2.
points.more: Scarborough-Rouge Park is lowest at 86, followed by Davenport at 86.3. University-Rosedale and York South-Weston are both at 87.9.

queries.purpose: Coyote-related 311 requests per year (2026 is partial)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(date) AS VARCHAR) || CASE WHEN year(date) = 2026 THEN ' (part year)' ELSE '' END AS label, sum(requests) AS value FROM service_requests_311 WHERE request_type ILIKE '%coyot%' GROUP BY year(date) ORDER BY year(date) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Coyote-related 311 requests by month of year, full years 2019-2025
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(date, '%b') AS label, sum(requests) AS value FROM service_requests_311 WHERE request_type ILIKE '%coyot%' AND year(date) BETWEEN 2019 AND 2025 GROUP BY month(date), strftime(date, '%b') ORDER BY month(date) LIMIT 12

story.lead: Coyote calls nearly doubled in 2025.
story.sub: Animal Services coyote requests 2023 to 2 Oct 2026 and 311 coyote requests 2019 to Aug 2026.

stat.caption: coyote requests to Animal Services in 2025, up from 3,088 in 2024

points.h: Animal Services coyote requests jumped in 2025
points.p: Requests rose from 2,781 in 2023 to 5,399 in 2025.
points.more: 2024 had 3,088 requests. 2026 already has 3,837 so far, with the year not yet finished.

points.h: 311 coyote requests have climbed since 2021
points.p: 311 coyote requests grew from 88 in 2021 to 498 in 2025.
points.more: 2019 and 2020 each had 127. 2026 has 369 so far, and the year is not over.

points.h: Coyote requests show no strong season
points.p: Across 2019 to 2025, every month had between 101 and 173 requests.
points.more: July was highest with 173, followed by November with 168. June was lowest with 101, then January with 104.

queries.purpose: Serious collisions by hour of day
queries.sql: SELECT lpad(CAST(hour(collision_time) AS VARCHAR), 2, '0') || ':00' AS label, count(DISTINCT collision_id) AS value FROM ksi_collisions WHERE collision_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY hour(collision_time) ORDER BY hour(collision_time)

queries.purpose: Serious collisions by day of week
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(collision_time, '%A') AS label, count(DISTINCT collision_id) AS value FROM ksi_collisions WHERE collision_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(collision_time, '%A'), isodow(collision_time) ORDER BY isodow(collision_time)

queries.purpose: Serious collisions by month of year (all years combined)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(collision_time, '%b') AS label, count(DISTINCT collision_id) AS value FROM ksi_collisions WHERE collision_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(collision_time, '%b'), month(collision_time) ORDER BY month(collision_time)

story.lead: Evenings, Fridays and summer-to-autumn months.
story.sub: 7,620 serious collisions (someone killed or seriously injured) in Toronto, 2006 to September 2026.

points.h: The evening rush hour is the peak
points.p: Serious collisions climb through the afternoon and peak at 6pm.
points.more: The 6pm hour has 531 collisions, followed by 507 at 5pm. The three hours from 5pm to 8pm hold 1,491 collisions, about 20% of all. The quietest hour is 4am, with 84.

points.h: Friday is the worst day
points.p: Weekdays see more serious collisions than the weekend, with Friday highest.
points.more: Friday has 1,216 collisions and Sunday has the fewest at 966. Tuesday and Wednesday are close behind Friday, at 1,138 and 1,127.

points.h: June to October is the busiest stretch
points.p: Serious collisions rise from spring and stay high until autumn.
points.more: June is highest with 774 collisions, and September (771) and August (753) are close. February is lowest at 455, so June has about 70% more.
